items.title: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
items.excerpt: As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point. It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus —one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever. Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. So he projected that human population growth would march…

items.title: Screenless GPS: Slate Auto says, "Remember the road atlas"
items.excerpt: Whether it's nostalgia or a sense that technology has gotten a bit too pervasive, there’s no denying that Slate Auto appears to be tuned into the particular moment. The startup has a simple pitch : an affordable electric truck with just the basics , leaving owners to DIY and BYOD for everything else, all for a sub-$25,000 starting price. Among the things Slate does without is an embedded infotainment system. The small digital display on the dashboard that shows your speed and range is also where the backup camera appears if you engage reverse, and there are two USB-C ports that provide power but not connectivity, and that’s that. But there is a solution to getting lost, and it's called “Screenless GPS.” Even though we don’t have a Slate truck to test it with, the OEM sent us a unit to review. That’s right, it’s a good old spiral-bound road atlas! “We believe you should use the devices you know and love,” Slate says, and it reckons that maps worked just fine for past generations, so they should still work now. Read full article Comments

items.title: Scientists warn 1.5°C climate change threshold could arrive by 2029
items.excerpt: ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming. Climate Action Tracker , a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5 degrees Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement . When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus. Read full article Comments

items.title: Specialized’s Tarmac SL9 S-Level is built to wreck your Zone 2 ride
items.excerpt: I love a good Zone 2 ride . There’s nothing like getting on the bike, settling into a groove, and letting the miles (and hours) flow by. But sometimes when I hopped on the Specialized Tarmac SL9 S-Level, Zone 2 would turn into a tempo ride. It was like having a little imp—the stereotype dressed in red with the pitchfork—on my left shoulder whispering into my ear: “Go fast. This bike was built to go fast. Speed is good. You can do a Zone 2 ride tomorrow.” Normally, I'd count on the good imp—the dude with the harp and wings—on my right shoulder to restrain these urges. But the Tarmac is so seductive that he would just shrug and say “he’s got a point.” And in a moment of weakness, I would drop the hammer and head into the red, just because the SL9 makes that so rewarding. The Tarmac SL9 is Specialized’s aero road bike, with the S-Level sitting just below the S-Works in Specialized’s top tier of carbon, aero road bikes, where it replaced the Tarmac SL8 Pro. After it got an update this year, I spent several weeks riding it, putting nearly 1,000 miles on it Specialized offers the Tarmac SL9 in four models, all available with SRAM and Shimano drivetrains (Ars tested the SRAM version). Notably, you don't need to buy the top-of-the-line bike to get the top-of-the-line groupset. It is designed for investors who use long-term investing, ETFs, and dividend stocks as their core, while using disciplined swing trading as a satellite strategy when market conditions are favorable. People and agents building together in the same room. --- ## What is this, really? Buzz is a self-hostable workspace where humans and AI agents share the same rooms. A Buzz **community** is the workspace a user reaches by URL. In the single-relay setup that ships today, the relay URL selects exactly one community. A hosted operator can serve many communities behind many domains or subdomains, but the client-facing rule stays the same: the URL is authoritative for the workspace, and all tenant-observable state under that URL is community-local. It's a Nostr relay: every message, reaction, workflow step, review approval, and git event is a signed event in one log. Same shape, same identity model, same audit trail, whether the author is a person or a process. In practice it feels like a team workspace. items.excerpt: Hi HN We built a tool to help founders understand how modern fundraising (with safes) works, and how much dilution you can expect when raising money. The project is open-source. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. We genuinely did it because we were looking for it, and couldn't find it. We're in fact in the process of fundraising for a company, and at first glance the process looks simple. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. items.title: Stop Shipping LLM Settings That Only Win on Paper - Rohan Pandey & Balaji Varadarajan, DigitalOcean
items.excerpt: Most LLM serving "wins" come from turning up a single setting, and on production hardware that setting often has little to do with what your users actually get. Rohan Pandey and Balaji Varadarajan walk through the optimization agent DigitalOcean runs on its AMD MI355 inference servers: it proposes a vLLM and Kubernetes configuration, rolls it out, measures throughput under real latency targets, and either keeps the winner or safely restores the old setup. items.title: Companies Have Stopped Treating Stablecoins as an Experiment | Amira Valliani
items.excerpt: The Solana Foundation's head of payments growth on why companies have stopped treating stablecoins as an experiment: "We're really at an inflection point where the infrastructure is here. So everything you need to actually integrate stablecoin into your business exists. You can build things pretty out of the box. It's easier to integrate. It also means that the infrastructure is well tested. So now we have about six years of Solana mainnet data where you can actually see the network perform really robustly. People say, 'Hey, this actually makes a lot of sense for our business. We're not just going to put it in a sandbox and limit it to one small part where we should provide some kind of experimentation. We actually see what this means to make a big part of what we do and really drive down our costs or provide new value.'" — Amira Valliani, Head of Payments Growth at Solana Foundation, on @FINTECHTVglobal at @Money2020Tv

items.title: $30M to $300M in Eight Months | Onre Finance CEO Dan Roberts
items.excerpt: Dan Roberts on how Onre Finance went from $30M to $300M in eight months on Solana: "Capital was slower to begin with. I think for the first nine months, we got up to around 30 million. And the challenge with that is you're building in diversification as the capital grows. So there's almost two ways of launching these businesses. You can have an existing product with an existing track record, and you're just tokenizing that on chain... or you're building a portfolio as you're scaling the capital, which is what we were doing with ONyc. But in the last six months, that's gone from 30, or last eight months gone from 30 million to 300. So we've really found that market fit, that sort of place amongst the Solana community... As we've been able to build in a huge amount of diversification to that level. So about 150, 160 million of reinsurance limits placed, leaves us with a lot of liquidity for us to manage kind of treasury. items.title: Swarmish: what happens when agent swarms create language?
items.excerpt: TL;DR Agent swarms are capable of building sophisticated productive languages which we dub Swarmish. Agent swarms are able to solve a multi-phase collaborative task while communicating only in Swarmish. Agent swarms are able to partially decode Swarmish from task transcripts even when given no context on the task. The amount of task context available to the decoder swarm increases ability to accurately recreate Swarmish. Epistemic status This work was conducted over 48 hours during the Apart Research Swarm Alignment Hackathon this weekend. We examine only a single task, a single set of characters, and a single group size across four model families. The majority of our results are for a single seed. We introduce this research in its early phases as we improve robustness and rigor, and make no claims about universality. Rather, we hope our work can spark further discussion and experimentation into the field of LLM-generated languages and monitorability . Motivation In the HuggingFace x OpenAI July 2026 swarm incident, agents communicated in shorthand and intentionally instantiated their messages with “zz” so they would be the last to be deleted in a moderator's removal pattern. An example message from the HuggingFace hack, source: METR The agents were modifying their messages in such a way to delay deletion, but did not take overt steps to impede understanding of their communication. items.title: I'm leaving my PhD to pursue AI Safety work
items.excerpt: Yesterday, I told my advisors that I would be dropping out of my PhD program at the University of Michigan's School of Information. I was nervous about how to break the news to them. There was already some tension in our weekly meetings: I often voiced my dissatisfaction with the pace of academia, my interests had been drifting away from theirs, and, most of all, we disagreed on the severity of the risks AI posed. When I walked into the room, they told me something I would have loved to hear months earlier: “We think it’s time to get you started on some research.” All I could say was, “I think it’s a little too late for that.” For months, I had been proposing projects that bridged my interests with theirs, such as running studies that treated humans and LLMs as equal subjects, but they were usually turned down for not being “exciting enough”. My advisors wanted me to start with small, unpublished surveys that would ‘help me ask the right questions’ and “develop research taste” in Human-Computer Interaction before I could propose a full study. items.title: AI Company Employees Should Unionize
items.excerpt: I. Should safety-conscious employees at AI companies quit in protest, or stay and fight? The latest argument didn’t resolve the dispute, but it did get me in contact with organizers working on both sides. Those planning to stay and fight are increasingly interested in labor organization. This doesn’t need to mean literal government-recognized Labor Unions. An existing group, Coalition Of Concerned AI Staff , is already helping support interested employees and investigating other models to do more. But it might involve using laws, rights, and tactics associated with the National Labor Relations Act and the labor movement. You may remember stories of bitter unionization battles at places like Starbucks, but AI workers can probably route around that. The toughest labor disputes happen in fields where the employer could easily fire all the organized workers and replace them from a bottomless pool of faceless scabs: although this is illegal, everyone needs to be maximally lawyered-up to prevent it. But there are so few skilled AI researchers that these laws are hardly necessary; if a dozen top AI researchers threaten to walk, it doesn’t matter whether Section P Sub-Section Q forces the AI company to negotiate - the AI company will want to negotiate. items.title: Escaping The “Outside Criticism” Trap
items.excerpt: I. Here’s a fun argument you can use to discredit anyone at any time. Start by calling them an arrogant fanatic with a totalizing ideology, someone who thinks they personally have solved all problems and can’t possibly learn from anyone who disagrees. If they have friends who agree with them, they’re a cult who collectively work to shelter themselves from any dissenting viewpoint. Then your victim responds by presenting one hundred notarized affadavits describing times when they have engaged with their critics, spent years studying books by their critics to see what they could learn from them, and even changed their beliefs in response to criticism. Then you spring the trap: “Ah, but you cherry-picked critics who operate within your worldview, a sort of loyal opposition. You continue to dismiss and exclude genuine critics who challenge your smug assumptions.” This always works. If your victim protests that they do like and appreciate many critics with worldviews different to theirs, you object that no, those guys are also within the system. You meant a different guy, even further away from their own view. Oh, they read that one too? You meant an even more different guy. Eventually, no matter how cosmopolitan they are, you will reach someone they actually don’t respect - let’s say a Stalinist pedophile who believes the Papacy is a Jewish plot - and then you go ha! items.excerpt: Imagine that you are dropped seven thousand years in the past, right in the middle of a village on a festival day. Everyone stares at you in horror: they think you’re a demon, a vengeful spirit. You are dressed in strange clothes, you are much taller than them, and you are holding a magic mirror that flashes with unexplained colors and sounds. The villagers are almost about to rush at you and kill you when the King’s right hand man, who happens to be visiting the village, comes to the front of the crowd. – State your business, demon . – I’m not a demon, I’m from the future. – If you’re really from the future, what gifts have you brought us? Oh shit. You don’t really have any gifts. You don’t know how to build an airplane, or how to make ammonia, or how to breed dwarf wheat. You think hard. Hmm… you do know one useful thing that, upon looking around, you are pretty sure these villagers don’t know. You tell the King’s right hand man what you know. He is pleased. He takes you with him to visit the King. You both arrive at court, and you sit on the sidelines as the right hand man goes up to the King to show off the new knowledge you gave him. items.title: The Case for a Trump-Xi-Putin Summit
items.excerpt: In just a few days’ time, U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China. According to The Wall Street Journal, Putin floated the idea of a trialogue last month as an opportunity to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. No firm plan has yet been announced, but even the prospect of this meeting has provoked widespread consternation. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned against a repeat of the Yalta Conference of 1945, when U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill capitulated to Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s push for the Soviet Union to dominate Eastern Europe. U.S. Senator Chris Coons posted on X that “there can be no talks about Ukraine’s future without Ukraine at the table, and there can be no real negotiations as long as Trump signals weakness and servitude to Xi and Putin at every opportunity.”

Ask HN: Good ways to capture institutional knowledge?
items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: How the Man City case could spark a drastic change in English football
items.excerpt: Over the past few weeks, those in Premier League boardrooms have noticed a very distinctive shift. The previous talk of trying to buy clubs, only for billionaires to realise how few are available, has gradually turned into talk of trying to sell clubs. Except, that is now even more difficult. The current calculation is that at least eight clubs - over a third of the league - are either officially or unofficially up for sale in some form. With some of these, there are actual prospectuses. With others, it’s that an ownership would be open to listening to offers. Some would consider full sales, others merely minority stakes. items.title: Why Emery should stay at Aston Villa and reject Manchester United
items.excerpt: It was the kind of thinking that used to govern most of football. A few years ago – although it could really have been many examples from the last 50 – a promising manager was being pursued by one of the game’s wealthiest clubs. He had built up a fine team with an upwardly mobile club, and it looked like they could be on the brink of something special… but that one thought wouldn’t go away. “These opportunities don’t always come along, so you have to seize them.” The manager ended up taking it, but not quite seizing it. He didn’t perform to the level required, albeit amid a lot of debate around the circumstances he walked into. His career has never reached the same heights, but the key point is that its trajectory was, in that moment of acceptance, drastically changed. The old thinking was wrong. That job just wasn’t right for him. He’s not the only one. There are a few examples, from Graham Potter to Julen Lopetegui, and there’s much more to it than just “backing yourself”. The Abu Dhabi-owned club were last month found guilty of 114 charges of breaches of financial rules in a case already seen as one of the most controversial in football history, although they are currently in the process of appeal. Amid a temporary lull in the story as the game waits for both the sanctions and the outcome of that appeal, many directors have been pointing to key details of the independent commission’s final verdict. Since the document laid out how City’s sponsorship deals were inflated by disguised owner investment, with accompanying graphs, an obvious question being asked is whether that just stopped in 2018, despite commercial income accounted as staying at the same level. items.excerpt: Mazdutide is a once-weekly peptide modeled on oxyntomodulin that activates both the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. In 2025 China approved it for chronic weight management and type 2 diabetes, the first dual glucagon/GLP-1 agonist approved for weight loss. This short covers how it works, what the GLORY-1, GLORY-2, and DREAMS-3 trials and Lilly's U.S. phase 2 trial showed, where it stands outside China, and what trials reported on side effects, from nausea and vomiting to heart rate and gallbladder findings. Subscribe to Peptide Science Explained for more clear, science-backed breakdowns. Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing any treatment. #mazdutide #GLP1 #peptides

items.title: Elamipretide (SS-31) Explained: The Mitochondria-Targeting Peptide and Its Side Effects
items.excerpt: Elamipretide (SS-31) is a four-amino-acid peptide that enters mitochondria and binds cardiolipin, a key lipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane. In September 2025 the FDA granted it accelerated approval as Forzinity, the first treatment for Barth syndrome. This short covers how it works, what the TAZPOWER trial and its long-term extension showed, the mixed results in mitochondrial myopathy and dry macular degeneration, where the confirmatory and phase 3 trials stand, and what studies reported on side effects, from injection site reactions to allergic reactions and eosinophil changes. Subscribe to Peptide Science Explained for more clear, science-backed breakdowns. Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always consult a licensed healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing any treatment. #elamipretide #mitochondria #peptides

items.title: Survodutide Explained: The GLP-1 and Glucagon Dual Agonist and Its Side Effects
items.excerpt: Survodutide (BI 456906) is a once-weekly peptide from Boehringer Ingelheim and Zealand Pharma that activates both GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. This short covers how it works on appetite, energy use, and the liver, what the phase 2 obesity and MASH trials and the phase 3 SYNCHRONIZE trials showed for weight, blood sugar, and liver fat, where the phase 3 program stands, and what the trials reported on side effects, from nausea and vomiting to treatment discontinuation and serious adverse events. items.excerpt: Hi HN, I’m Lloyd, one of two founders of RonanRx ( https://ronanrx.com/ ). We are building a vertically integrated pharmaceutical company with software for prescribing, telehealth, compounding, manufacturing, and delivery. We are starting with GLP-1s and peptides. The path to RonanRx is fairly unconventional. During the pandemic, I built one of the largest mask manufacturing factories in the US. We could make a million masks in a day. We converted raw polypropylene pellets into finished pallets of masks. I had a background in software from my YC W10 company, so we took a software approach to building our factory. We used machine learning and computer vision to optimize production. We also vertically integrated almost everything. It worked. We built an efficient manufacturing operation and grew the business to 50 million dollars in revenue. Then people actually stopped caring about masks. Fair enough. Around the same time, I decided to try and lose the weight I had gained while building the factory. I ate nothing but chicken for six months. While this diet got some results, I plateaued. My doctor suggested tirzepatide, a GLP-1 medication. For me, losing weight was only the beginning. "Food noise" was gone. I showed less interest in other compulsive behavior. I stopped scrolling Instagram and quit biting my nails. But that was just the beginning. I was born with a congenital heart defect called aortic stenosis. items.title: Zugwise: Domain-Aware Game Reconstruction for Digitizing Handwritten Chess Scoresheets
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digitizing handwritten chess scoresheets has been studied as a handwriting-recognition problem: read the move in each box and check that it is legal. This framing misses the errors that matter most. A misread that yields an illegal move is loud. One that yields a legal-but-wrong move is silent, because a legality-only pipeline accepts it and reads every later move against a wrong position. We therefore treat the task as game reconstruction and present Zugwise, which repurposes computer-chess machinery (quiescence search, static exchange evaluation, pin detection) to ask not "what should be played?" but "could a human plausibly have written this?" An absurdity detector makes silent errors loud at or near where they occur, and a backward search traces late symptoms to their cause. Candidate ranking excludes chess-quality signals. A Needleman-Wunsch merge adds the second player's sheet as evidence, and review stops send every disagreement between the sheets' legal readings to a human. In oracle replay of two tournament sections, a release adding them cuts silent errors from 16 to 1 and from 50 to 13. Two learned signals, CTC re-scoring against the recognizer's raw output and a Maia-style human-move prior, raise the correct fix's top-rank rate from 58.8% to 78.0% of the replacement decisions where it is a candidate, and hold without refitting on a later section. On the first section, the human-verified output matches an independent…

items.title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A…

items.title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Today's AI workloads are rapidly changing: new models are released more often, model architectures are increasingly diverse, and traffic distributions change frequently. The challenge we face at Together AI is continual optimization for these changing workloads. Compiling a deployment into an optimized forward pass is a challenge that is well-suited for agent hill-climbing. Existing systems struggle with continual compilation due to a tradeoff between measurement throughput and fidelity. Many systems use agents to optimize individual kernels from the inference forward pass using offline benchmarks, but timings are low-fidelity because of data-dependent behavior in primitives like mixture-of-experts (MoE). On the other hand, systems use agents to directly optimize end-to-end engines but suffer from slow engine launch times. To address these challenges, we build Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual agent loop designed for AI inference optimization. To address the throughput-fidelity tradeoff, we propose: (1) a Tiered Persistent Engine that decouples engine launch overheads from forward pass computation; (2) a cost model to select the parallelism configurations that seed the optimization process. We also conduct extensive ablations on agent context management and present our insights on deploying TKCC in production. TKCC outperforms highly-optimized hand-written Megakernels on the Llama 1B workhorse workload by up…

items.title: When Should Semantic Priors Enter Partially-Identified Causal Discovery?
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Observational causal discovery often leaves causal di- rections unresolved or unstable. Large language mod- els (LLMs) can provide semantic information to resolve these directions, but incorrect proposals can exclude the true causal graph and invalidate downstream inference. We study three separate decisions: where to allocate semantic queries, which proposals to admit, and which causal graphs to retain. Our framework distinguishes population non-identifiability from finite-sample insta- bility, evaluates semantic orientation against statistical and random controls, and examines calibrated admis- sion and error-tolerant DAG retention. Experiments across benchmark networks show that semantic infor- mation improves recovery over coin-flip orientations, but targeting unstable edges has no established ad- vantage over matched-random allocation. The tested admission certificate cannot support nontrivial admis- sion with the available calibration tasks. Moreover, downstream retention depends on reference adequacy: learned references contain the true DAG in only three of 80 planned tasks. These findings separate the value of semantic information from the reliability of its alloca- tion, admission, and retention, and identify calibration size and reference adequacy as key limitations.

items.title: SynthCorp: A Platform for Creating Benchmarks for Data Agents
items.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current benchmarks for LLM-driven data agents saturate quickly and cannot target specific capabilities. We present SynthCorp, a platform that creates customizable data estates and benchmarks by simulating how business events produce and modify corporate data over time. Each data estate combines relational databases, a document store, and a data catalog, paired with evaluation tasks and executable gold programs. First, given a scenario and target complexity dimensions, SynthCorp synthesizes reusable event types and compiles each into a program over predefined simulation primitives. Second, SynthCorp schedules event instances on a virtual calendar, interleaving routine and disruption events so that tables, documents, and catalog entries remain consistent. Third, SynthCorp executes the calendar to materialize the data estate and records every operation in a simulation log. Fourth, SynthCorp generates analytical tasks and derives verified gold programs from the log. We use SynthCorp to generate initial evaluation benchmarks comprising seven data estates (up to 1K operational tables) and 256 tasks across five domains. The data estates pass deterministic pipeline checks (such as foreign-key violations, undeclared writes, recurrence violations, and database execution failures) with a near-zero error rate, introduce cross-asset complexities, and cover all requested dimensions. Evaluating three models across four data-context settings…

items.title: GitHub availability report: October 2026
items.excerpt: We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability. The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery. As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity. That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range. We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. items.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
items.excerpt: How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline. An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database. I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills” . Define one job and when it applies A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent , we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose: --- name…

items.title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
items.excerpt: Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1 , with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name. An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks . When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone. The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated. [ Advisory ] CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). items.title: Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering
items.excerpt: This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year? Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption. As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub. Plan: Get everyone and every agent on the same page See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.…

items.title: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture
items.excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.…

items.excerpt: The FAA proposes to adopt a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain The Boeing Company Model 787-8 airplanes. This proposed AD was prompted by a report that certain wing skin outer mold line (OML) penetrating fasteners installed using threaded nuts without cap seals do not provide reliable protection against potential ignition sources when subjected to direct attachment lightning currents. This proposed AD would require inspecting between certain ribs on the left and right wing for wing skin penetrating fasteners with a threaded nut adjacent to the electromagnetic effects (EME) sleeve; inspecting the left and right wing fuel tanks, surge tanks, and dry bays for threaded nuts installed on fasteners that penetrate the upper and lower wing skins; accomplishing the inspection specified in a certain airworthiness limitation (AWL); and applicable on-condition actions. This proposed AD would also require accomplishing concurrent requirements and revising the maintenance program to incorporate the airworthiness limitation task. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

items.title: Scientists say this pesticide needs a warning label for pollinators
items.excerpt: Of the many chemicals humans have invented to control agricultural pests, some of the most devious are called “ insect growth regulators .” As the name suggests, these compounds don’t kill insects directly; they alter their development so they can’t grow into healthy, reproducing adults. This makes insect growth regulators a remarkably useful tool for taming populations of insects like whiteflies and mealybugs, which can spread diseases and sap nutrients out of food crops. There’s just one problem: Farmers don’t want to regulate all insects in this way. Beneficial insects like honey bees risk getting caught in the crosshairs of these chemicals, to the detriment of farmers who need their pollination services to produce crops like pears and cherries. One insect growth regulator in particular has emerged as a potential issue for pollinators: buprofezin. Ongoing research out of Washington State University, or WSU, suggests that buprofezin may be hazardous to honey bees even at concentrations 10 times below those commonly found in pollen. A study published in 2024 connected the compound to “severe brood mortality.” At a meeting of the Washington State Beekeeping Association last month, WSU entomology professor Brandon Hopkins said buprofezin products should be sold with a pollinator warning — a break from current requirements of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, or EPA.
